name: Minas Gerais
summary_text: Minas Gerais is a state within Brazil and stands under the national framework set out for that country: same-sex marriage legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal's 2018 removal of the surgical requirement for legal gender change, an equal age of consent regardless of sexual orientation, and, since the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions under which discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds are punished and transphobia is treated on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's documents and family-law status are handled the same as anyone else's at entry.  The dominant visitor-facing risk in Minas Gerais is lethal violence against trans people, and the state sits at the severe end of the national picture. The ANTRA dossier for 2024, published 27 January 2025, ranks Minas Gerais second nationally with 12 trans killings during the year, behind São Paulo with 16 and ahead of Ceará with 11. The cumulative count for the state across 2017 to 2024 is 100.  The following year's figures put the state at the head of the national ranking. The ANTRA dossier for 2025, reported on 26 January 2026, records Minas Gerais tied with Ceará in first place with 8 trans killings during 2025, within a national total of 80.  Detention in the state operates under a defined federal rule-set. A portaria issued on 17 April 2014 by the Secretaria de Direitos Humanos da Presidência da República sets housing rules for LGBT prisoners across Brazil's prison system and applies within the Minas Gerais state prison system. Transsexual men and women must be forwarded to female prison units, gay and travesti prisoners held in male prisons must be offered specific conviviality spaces, and LGBT inmates may use their social name, which must appear in the admission record, together with the choice of male or female clothing.

name: Para
summary_text: Pará stands under Brazil's national framework: same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and federal anti-discrimination provisions cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds. After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on those grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's documents and family status are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry.  Arrest and imprisonment in Pará fall under a specific national regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. Status is recognised by self-declaration before a judge, including at the custody hearing. On arrest the judge fixes the place of deprivation of liberty in a reasoned decision after consulting the person, setting out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and recording whether a trans, travesti or intersex person prefers a female, male or specific unit and, within it, the general population or a designated wing or cell. The declared preference stands, later changes of placement are possible, transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat, LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.  Killing is the dominant documented risk. The 9th annual dossier of ANTRA, the national trans rights organisation, records 80 trans and travesti people killed across Brazil in 2025, a fall of about 34% year-on-year, while the country remains ranked first in world rankings for such killings. The victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence. Pará accounts for 5 of those 80 victims in 2025.  The comparison year is larger: ANTRA's dossier recorded 122 trans and travesti killings nationally in 2024, 16% below 2023, with five of the victims rights defenders. Pará's 2024 position cannot be fixed from the available sources.  Protection on paper does not describe routine experience. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A trans visitor therefore enters a jurisdiction where documents, marriage and entry treatment are equal under law, while physical safety risk is measured by a national homicide record in which Brazil ranks first worldwide.
